response.rationale: D4 (Pemphigus foliaceus) is favored because the biopsy shows acantholytic keratinocytes and intercellular IgG/C3 in the upper epidermis, which are pathognomonic for pemphigus foliaceus. The photodistributed pattern and positive ANA are less specific but compatible. D6 (Pemphigus) is broader and includes pemphigus vulgaris, which typically has lower epidermal involvement and mucosal lesions; the upper epidermal deposition and lack of mucosal involvement point to foliaceus. Lupus variants (D1, D2, D5, D7, D9) do not explain acantholysis and intercellular immunoglobulin deposition. D3 and D8 lack key histologic and immunofluorescence findings.

rejected.why: Lupus erythematosus tumidus lacks acantholysis and intercellular IgG/C3 deposition; histology shows dermal infiltrate without epidermal acantholysis.
Discoid lupus erythematosus typically shows follicular plugging, atrophy, and basement membrane thickening, not acantholysis and intercellular immunoglobulin.
Sjögren's syndrome does not explain acantholytic keratinocytes or intercellular IgG/C3 deposition; skin lesions are not typical.
Lupus erythematosus is too broad and does not account for acantholysis and intercellular immunoglobulin pattern; anti-Ro/La negative argues against SCLE.
Pemphigus is a broader category; the upper epidermal intercellular deposition and lack of mucosal involvement favor foliaceus over vulgaris, so D4 is more specific.
Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus typically has interface dermatitis and anti-Ro/La antibodies, which are negative here; acantholysis is not a feature.
Dermatomyositis presents with heliotrope rash and Gottron papules, not acantholysis or intercellular immunoglobulin deposition.
Systemic lupus erythematosus may have ANA and cytopenias but does not explain acantholysis and intercellular IgG/C3; histology is not consistent.

His prosthesis was extruded from his socket due to cicatricial effects causing conjunctival shrinkage and eyelid skin contracture.

vignette:
A 76-year-old man with numerous cardiovascular comorbid conditions presented with weeks of worsening renal function leading to hospitalization. Home medications included rosuvastatin, aspirin, prasugrel, sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, ezetimibe, furosemide, and ferrous sulfate. vignette:
A woman in her 40s presented with blurred vision in the right eye. She was undergoing treatment with systemic steroids, durvalumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor), and bevacizumab. Ten days after initial presentation, the patient developed sudden vision loss in the right eye.

vignette:
A 78-year-old man presented with painful swelling and ulceration of the glans penis of 1 month's duration. His medical history included an elevated white blood cell count and inguinal lymphadenopathy discovered 9 years prior. Four years after initial presentation, he experienced fatigue, weight loss, and loss of appetite. The current illness began 1 month prior to admission when he noticed asymptomatic 'green-yellow welts' and swelling of the glans penis. The swelling became progressively painful and evolved to the size of an 'orange' over 4 days. Previous treatments with topical antibiotics, antifungal agents, hydrogen peroxide soaks, warm compresses, and cephalexin showed no improvement.

Patient appeared healthy. The glans penis and corona were grossly edematous, with a 3.7 × 3.3-cm tender, firm ulcer on the ventral surface of the penis with overlying black eschar, adherent yellow crust, and granulation tissue. No urethral discharge was present.

- Laboratory Tests: Routine blood test results were within normal limits. Cultures, assays, and blood tests evaluating for viral, bacterial, or fungal etiology were negative.

- Pathology Studies: Biopsy of the glans penis ulcer showed dermal infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes, which were CD20+, CD79a+, and CD5+, within the background of a reactive T-cell infiltrate. PCR analysis revealed a clonal IgH gene rearrangement.

- Imaging Studies: PET-CT scan demonstrated FDG-avid abdominal and peripancreatic lymph nodes.

vignette:
A 65-year-old woman presented with blurry vision in her right eye for several months. Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. Patient had undergone left-sided mastectomy 2.5 years prior and had been on anastrozole therapy for more than 2 years. Medical history and past medication use were otherwise unremarkable.

Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/150 OS without improvement on pinhole testing. Intraocular pressures were normal. Right eye showed trace conjunctival injection without definite ciliary flush, 2+ fine keratic precipitates, and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Left eye had a few keratic precipitates. Dilated fundus examination revealed cystoid macular edema with a yellow spot in the fovea in the right eye and an epiretinal membrane in the left eye. No inflammation in the periphery was noted in either eye.

vignette:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

vignette:
A 39-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of persistent fever, night sweats, a 15-kg weight loss, decreased appetite, dry cough, and shortness of breath. He had no significant medical history, no recent travel, and no known sick contacts, but lived in close quarters with 13 other inmates. On examination, his heart rate was elevated, blood pressure was low but responsive to fluids, and he had fine tremors. Laboratory studies showed hyponatremia, elevated liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP), and raised inflammatory markers. Anteroposterior chest radiography revealed numerous bilateral tiny nodules throughout both lung fields. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed innumerable widespread pulmonary nodules, a few cavitary lesions, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. vignette:
A 47‐year‐old woman presented with crescendo chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath on exertion for two days. In the emergency department she was hypotensive, tachycardic, and tachypneic. Physical examination showed bilateral fine basal crepitations, a grade 2 decrescendo diastolic murmur, and bilateral pitting lower‐limb edema. She was an active smoker working in warehouse logistics, with no history of substance misuse or family history of cardiovascular disease.

Chest radiography demonstrated congested basal lung fields with mild bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment depressions in the inferior leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed anterior‐wall hypokinesia and moderate‐to‐severe aortic insufficiency; immobile echogenic shadows in the ascending aorta obscured the aortic valve. A computed tomography aortogram excluded aortic dissection. Urgent coronary angiography via the radial approach showed a slit-like left main coronary ostium while the remainder of the coronary arteries was free of atherosclerotic plaque.

These atypical findings prompted investigations for infectious and inflammatory aortitis. Potential causative organisms under consideration included Treponema pallidum, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Salmonella species, Staphylococcus species, and Campylobacter jejuni. Musculoskeletal examination and immunological assays were not suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or Behçet disease.

vignette:
A 41-year-old woman with a 3-month history of sacroiliac pain, arthralgias, and lower-limb myalgias partially responsive to NSAIDs was diagnosed with seronegative spondyloarthropathy (negative HLA-B27) after MRI confirmed bilateral active sacroiliitis. Two months later, she began weekly subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg with significant improvement in her joint symptoms. After the third dose, she developed a dry cough and dyspnea on moderate exertion without fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, or other systemic symptoms. She denied tobacco use, recent travel, or exposures to animals, dusts, or sick contacts. 

On examination in the emergency department, she was afebrile, blood pressure 118/84 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygenation normal on room air. Pulmonary auscultation revealed scant basal “Velcro”-like crackles. Other exams were unremarkable apart from positive sacroiliac provocation tests. 

Laboratory studies: Hb 13 g/dL, WBC 4,100/mm³ (neutrophils 2,000, lymphocytes 1,400), eosinophils 50/mm³, platelets 325,000/mm³; AST, ALT, bilirubin, creatinine, and BUN were within normal limits. 

High-resolution chest CT showed ground-glass interstitial infiltrates with a centrifugal distribution, predominantly in the upper lobes, and a mosaic pattern of disseminated attenuation without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion. An echocardiogram was normal, and ECG showed sinus rhythm. 

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed no endobronchial lesions; GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and methenamine silver stain were negative.

vignette:
A 53-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and bipolar disorder was admitted for a 4-week history of progressive asthenia, anorexia, and a 7-kg weight loss, with vomiting during the last 2 days. On examination, her BMI was 18.2 kg/m2 and she was obnubilated; the ECG was normal. Laboratory studies showed:

• PTH 9 ng/L.

She received IV saline and one dose of zoledronate, with normalization of calcium and renal function by day 3. A CT scan of the body showed two osteolytic lesions of the left frontal and temporal skull bones, multiple hypodense micronodules in all hepatic segments, and multiple splenic nodules. Brain MRI demonstrated T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, gadolinium-enhancing lesions in the same skull regions. A DEXA scan revealed osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score –2.4). Mammography, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal. Bone marrow biopsy and labial salivary gland histology were unremarkable. A percutaneous fine-needle aspiration of the liver showed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis without malignancy. The intradermal tuberculin test was negative. During this period, hypercalcemia recurred, and two additional doses of zoledronate were administered 15 days apart despite initial correction.

vignette:
A 21-year-old man with no past medical or surgical history presented with a tender, palpable mass in his left buttock that he had noticed for several years but which had rapidly enlarged over the previous six months. He also reported recent onset of constipation and numbness of the left lower extremity, worsened by sitting. He denied any drainage, redness, fever, or systemic symptoms. He took no medications and had no family history of cancer.

On examination, a 4 × 4 cm tender mass was palpated in the left perineum without overlying skin changes. Neurologic examination showed hypoesthesia in the L5–S4 distribution on the left with intact motor function; the right lower extremity was normal. Abdominal and digital rectal examinations were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed a well-defined, nonenhancing, unilocular hypodense cystic lesion anterior to the rectum measuring 7.0 × 9.0 cm, as well as a separate 4.4 × 4.7 cm cyst in the left perineum. On contrast-enhanced MRI, both lesions appeared homogeneous, T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, and showed no wall enhancement. The cysts were distinct from the bladder, urethra, prostate, and rectum, and were suggested to have a narrow neck traversing the pelvic floor near the pudendal canal.

vignette:
A 30-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-week history of worsening crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and bloody diarrhea. She denied smoking or alcohol use. Her only medication was a progesterone-only contraceptive, which she had been taking for 2 months.

On examination, her temperature was normal, blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, heart rate 114 bpm, and BMI 32.3. Abdominal palpation revealed diffuse tenderness without guarding or rigidity; bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, metabolic panel, and coagulation studies; C-reactive protein was 4.8 mg/dL. Stool cultures and assays for Clostridioides difficile toxins were negative. Fecal calprotectin was elevated at 2006 µg/g (reference 10–50 µg/g).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated mild thickening of the mid- and distal descending colon with adjacent inflammatory stranding; there was no evidence of perforation, abscess, or diverticulosis.

She was treated with intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and pain medications, and received a single dose of ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. 

Colonoscopy revealed segmental erythema and ulceration in the descending and sigmoid colon, with normal-appearing mucosa in the ascending colon, transverse colon, and rectum. 

Biopsy specimens from the affected segments showed subepithelial edema, hemorrhage, mild crypt architectural distortion, and an acute inflammatory infiltrate without granulomas or dysplasia.

vignette:
A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history was noted by his parents to have a slowly developing limitation in right-eye movement over several weeks. There was no pain, inflammation, fever, trauma, or history of ocular infection, and his overall health was unchanged. On examination, abduction of the right eye was restricted. There were no signs of proptosis, strabismus, visual impairment, or inflammation in either eye; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies, including an infectious work-up, were negative.  
Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a well-circumscribed extraconal mass at the right superolateral orbital wall, adjacent to the frontozygomatic suture, with smooth bone remodeling and fluid-attenuating content but no bone invasion. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a cystic mass in the right superior extraconal compartment that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on FLAIR imaging, and exhibited no diffusion restriction or internal enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion exerted mild compression on the external and superior rectus muscles, correlating with the abduction deficit, but did not involve the optic nerve, intraconal fat, or show intracranial extension.

vignette:
A 39-year-old Ukrainian immigrant woman presented with approximately 1 year of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. She had no prior evaluations and was referred for upper endoscopy, which revealed a large antral mass; a mucosal biopsy was obtained, but she declined endoscopic ultrasound and was lost to follow-up during pregnancy. She later returned with ongoing anemia and new epigastric pain. Repeat esophagogastroduodenoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound identified a 6 cm mass arising from the muscularis propria of the gastric antrum. Preoperative computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 9.7 × 7.8 × 4.8 cm heterogeneous mass adherent to the posterior wall of the gastric antrum, with predominantly fat attenuation, internal septations, and no pathologic lymphadenopathy. She then presented with melena; a repeat endoscopy showed mucosal ulceration overlying the mass, and biopsy results were consistent with adipose tissue.

vignette:
A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. Transcranial Doppler confirmed tortuosity and plaques but demonstrated normal hemodynamics of the cerebro-afferent vessels. Repeat brain MRI showed no signs of recent vascular lesions.

vignette:
A 13-year-old girl was admitted with a 2-week history of progressive dysphagia, dyspnea, facial swelling, pallor, and fatigue. On examination, she had signs of superior vena cava syndrome. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6×10^9/L (48% lymphocytes, 42% neutrophils), hemoglobin 85 g/L, and C-reactive protein 117. Chest radiography revealed an anterior mediastinal mass extending to the hila. CT scan confirmed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the anterior mediastinum without other masses. The patient underwent surgical resection of the mediastinal lesions, yielding ten lymph nodes measuring 3–7 cm. Histologic sections showed effacement of nodal architecture by cohesive sheets of large pleomorphic cells with abundant cytoplasm, kidney-shaped nuclei, frequent mitoses, and occasional Reed–Sternberg–like cells. A 65-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of intermittent epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Her medical history was notable for poor mobility, type II diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. Eight years earlier, she had been admitted with Escherichia coli sepsis; an abdominal ultrasound at that time had incidentally shown a partially calcified gallbladder without signs of inflammation, and benign fatty changes in the liver. No intervention was pursued given her comorbidities.

On this admission, vital signs were within normal limits and general examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed no organomegaly or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed: ALT 45 U/L, ALP 775 U/L, total bilirubin 20 µmol/L, albumin 27 g/L, GGT 553 U/L, adjusted calcium 2.73 mmol/L, and a leukocyte count of 10.8×10^9/L.

The common bile duct was normal in calibre, with no intrahepatic duct dilatation. There was also a large, ill-defined heterogeneous mass within the liver.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 10-cm calcified gallbladder wall invading liver segments 4 and 5, enlarged coeliac, peri-pancreatic, and para-aortic lymph nodes, and multiple pulmonary nodules consistent with metastatic disease (T4 N1 M1).

A 45-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of an abrupt onset of an asymptomatic cutaneous eruption on the neck and both forearms. vignette:
A 19-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an episode of reduced consciousness while bathing. His parents reported that when lukewarm water was poured over his chest, he turned blue around the lips and began gasping for air. During this time, his eyes “rolled back,” and he did not interact with his parents. There were no clonic movements, and he did not respond to physical stimulation. He subsequently fell asleep for approximately 1 hour and was brought to the ED.

On arrival, he was alert and appeared well. There were no focal findings on examination, his development was appropriate, and laboratory studies—including a blood glucose level of 5.5 mmol/L—were normal. His parents reported similar, less profound episodes during bathing over the previous 2 weeks, in which his head would go back, his eyes would roll upward, and he would become floppy and limp for 2–3 minutes, followed by sleepiness. These episodes occurred only during bathing; contact with water in other settings did not provoke symptoms. He had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical or family history.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval. Bathing in lukewarm water while his vital signs were monitored provoked hypotonia, tachycardia, and brief apnea with associated desaturation. He stared straight ahead and made mouthing movements; he was removed from the bath, given high-flow oxygen, and again slept for about 1 hour. A further similar episode occurred later while he was sleeping, without any provocation. The first interictal EEG was normal using the standard 10–20 system. Because he was clinically well between episodes and there was an avoidable trigger, he was discharged with plans for follow-up investigations, including a brain MRI, a bathing EEG, and outpatient review.

vignette:
A 44-year-old woman from Veracruz, Mexico, of low socioeconomic status, with systemic lupus erythematosus since 2003 (cutaneous, joint, and renal involvement), presented with a one-week history of progressive headache, phonophobia, high-grade fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. One month earlier, she had been treated for SLE-associated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with plasmapheresis, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone at 1 mg/kg per day.

On admission she had systemic inflammatory response syndrome and nuchal rigidity but no focal neurologic deficits or clinical signs of lupus activity. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 103 fL, eosinophils 150 cells/mm3, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, haptoglobin 77 mg/dL, ALT 59 IU/L, AST 78 IU/L, LDH 310 mg/dL, C3 96.5 mg/dL, lactate 0.9 mmol/L, and proteinuria 310 mg/day. Chest radiograph and head CT were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed a pH of 7.35, glucose 45 mg/dL (serum glucose 130 mg/dL), protein 329 mg/dL, 42 white cells/mm3 (95% neutrophils), and 2 red cells/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grew Enterococcus gallinarum, and she was treated with intravenous ampicillin, with improvement in her neurologic symptoms.

On hospital day 3, she developed hemoptysis, bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph, a drop in hemoglobin concentration, and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU admission. Cultures were obtained, and she was started on methylprednisolone boluses and broad-spectrum antibiotics. The initial clinical diagnosis was diffuse alveolar hemorrhage caused by SLE activity without sufficient clinical criteria of nosocomial pneumonia.

On hospital day 4, she developed a purpuric skin rash, and a skin biopsy was performed.

vignette:
A 34-year-old North African woman with no significant past medical history was referred for management of obstructive jaundice. Two months earlier, she had undergone laparotomy and resection of the protruding dome of a segment I hepatic cyst thought to be a hydatid cyst compressing the biliary convergence. She now presented with fever to 38.5 °C, mucocutaneous jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. On examination, she was febrile and icteric; there was no abdominal tenderness, hepatomegaly, or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed moderate hepatocellular enzyme elevations and cholestasis. Hydatid serology and serum carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen levels were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a cystic lesion in segment I with parietal and septal enhancement and rupture into the biliary convergence. MRI demonstrated a multiloculated lesion that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, communicating with the biliary bifurcation, with dilatation of intrahepatic ducts (predominantly left) and of the common bile duct containing heterogeneous signal material. At laparotomy via a subcostal incision, the liver appeared micronodular; on opening the common bile duct, mucinous fluid and membranes were extracted, raising questions about the presumed diagnosis.

vignette:
A 43-year-old man presented with fever, chills, and headache. One month earlier, he had noted a painless ulcer on the prepuce that was healing when he developed fever and fatigue. Ten days before admission, he developed a disseminated maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. He reported multiple unprotected sexual contacts over the past three months. He is a man who has sex with men and was diagnosed with HIV infection 10 years ago; he takes abacavir, lamivudine, darunavir, ritonavir, and dolutegravir with an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 1144 cells/μL. One year ago, he was treated with intravenous penicillin G for suspected otosyphilis and had a full clinical and serologic response. 

On examination, he was ill-appearing but not dehydrated. He had painless enlargement of inguinal, axillary, and cervical lymph nodes (up to 3 cm) and a maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. He had a headache but no nuchal rigidity or Kernig or Brudzinsky signs.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 63,300/mL with a lymphomonocytic predominance. Blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and urine specific gravity were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 19 white cells (95% lymphocytes) with normal glucose and protein concentrations. Blood cultures were repetitively negative.

vignette:
A 60-year-old Ugandan woman, recently diagnosed with HIV and not yet on antiretroviral therapy, was brought to the hospital with a one-day history of reduced consciousness, abrupt onset of aphasia, and urinary incontinence. She also reported a two-day history of dry cough, drenching night sweats, and weight loss but denied fever, headache, neck stiffness, visual disturbances, photophobia, or seizures.

On examination, she appeared wasted (weight 40 kg) and was afebrile (36.6 °C). Vital signs were: blood pressure 120/74 mmHg, pulse 66 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Neurologically, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14/15, with dysarthria but no other focal deficits; neck was supple, and pupils were equal and reactive. Chest and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Two days before admission, a non-contrast brain CT scan showed multiple enhancing nodular white matter lesions with significant peri-lesional edema and midline shift, as well as several small subcortical non-enhancing hypoattenuating lesions suggestive of infarcts. Initial laboratory testing revealed a CD4 count of 6 cells/mm^3 and a positive serum cryptococcal antigen test with a titer of 1:320. Lumbar puncture was deferred given the CT findings.

vignette:
A 57-year-old man was admitted with a 1-month history of high fever, night sweats, and progressive back pain. He reported touching an unpasteurized sheep stomach with an injured hand about 1 month earlier. Initial outpatient therapy with oral cefprozil provided no lasting benefit. On admission, he had no fever but complained of worsening back pain and malaise.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7170/mm3 with 80% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/hour, a C-reactive protein level of 3.19 mg/dL, and a procalcitonin level of 0.21 ng/mL. A serological test for tuberculosis was negative. He was started on intravenous sulbactam–cefoperazone. On hospital day 6, blood cultures grew a Gram-negative bacillus. That same day, he developed weakness and numbness in both legs and difficulty with urination. Neurologic examination revealed grade 3/5 strength in the right lower limb, grade 4/5 in the left, hypertonia of both lower extremities, and tenderness on percussion and palpation of the T9 and T10 spinous processes.

Contrast-enhanced thoracic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an inflammatory lesion of the T9 lamina and a posterior epidural abscess compressing the spinal cord at T9–T10. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed osteolytic destruction of the neural arch of T9. He was transferred to the Department of Orthopedics for surgical management.

vignette:
A 4-year-old girl was brought for evaluation of a slowly enlarging mass on the dorsal aspect of her right wrist, first noted 2 months earlier. The lesion caused pain and discomfort but no functional limitation. There was no history of trauma, other lesions, or relevant family or medical history. On examination, a 1.5 × 1.5 cm firm, tender mass with intact overlying skin was located medial to Lister’s tubercle; wrist range of motion was normal, sensation was intact, and pulses were palpable. The mass moved with extension of the right index finger.  
Ultrasound showed a well-defined, multilobulated, mildly echogenic swelling measuring 1.5 × 1.0 × 0.5 cm with some vascularity, lying within the fourth extensor tendon compartment adjacent to the extensor indicis proprius tendon.  
Therefore, the working diagnosis was a giant‐cell tumor of the tendon sheath. No further imaging was performed.

vignette:
A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

vignette:
A 33-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a growing, painless nodule in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast. On examination, the lesion was firm, mobile, well defined, and without skin changes. There was no nipple discharge or palpable lymphadenopathy; the right breast was normal. Mammography showed a well-defined 33 × 26 mm mass with multiple pleomorphic calcifications that had increased in number compared with a prior study. Ultrasonography revealed a 3.5 cm hypoechoic, subcutaneous, poorly circumscribed nodule with marked posterior acoustic shadowing from microcalcifications and no locoregional lymphadenopathy. The lesion was classified as ACR BI-RADS IV.

vignette:
A 23-year-old man with end-stage renal disease due to IgA nephropathy, maintained on peritoneal dialysis (four exchanges daily; he had missed his last two), was brought to a community hospital after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He reported headache and blurred vision for several hours prior. On arrival he was combative and confused, with blood pressure >182/107 mmHg; he received labetalol 20 mg IV, lorazepam 1 mg IV, and haloperidol 1 mg IV before transfer.

At the tertiary care center: temperature 36.8 °C; blood pressure 200/100 mmHg; heart rate 63 bpm; oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was rousable but confused, alert to person and place. Neurologic exam, including language and fundoscopy, was normal; there was no meningismus. Cardiovascular exam revealed a loud S2; respiratory and abdominal exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed urea 41 mmol/L, creatinine 1531 μmol/L, WBC 11.4×10^9/L, hemoglobin 99 g/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 6.3 mmol/L, calcium 1.93 mmol/L, phosphate 3.57 mmol/L, magnesium 1.24 mmol/L; liver enzymes were normal. ECG demonstrated tall peaked T waves consistent with hyperkalemia. Noncontrast head CT revealed multiple cortical and subcortical hypodensities in the posterior parasagittal parietal lobes and the medial right occipital lobe, reported as suggestive of PRES.

vignette:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks 3 days of gestation presented with acute left lower abdominal pain and vomiting. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, constipation, or changes in bowel habits. Her observations were stable, and she appeared clinically well. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the left abdomen without guarding; the uterus was soft and relaxed. Foetal movements and monitoring were normal.

Her antenatal course had been uneventful except for a 70 × 60 × 60 mm left ovarian cyst first noted at 5 weeks and thought to be endometriotic. Follow-up scans at 32 weeks showed the cyst measured 63 × 33 × 69 mm with internal echoes and an avascular solid component. Tumour markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125) were within normal limits, and an MDT review deemed the cyst benign and recommended surveillance.

On admission, Hb was 121 g/L, WCC 10.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 270 × 10^9/L, and CRP 30 mg/L. Over three days, CRP rose to 209 mg/L while WCC remained stable. Repeated transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasounds by an experienced sonographer showed the left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance with no whirlpool sign, stromal oedema, absent Doppler flow, or free pelvic fluid. MRI was considered but not performed due to the rapid clinical change.

At 37 weeks 1 day, her pain worsened with vomiting, and abdominal exam revealed generalized tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa. Given the acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers, and concern for ovarian torsion, the decision was made to proceed with a caesarean section followed by surgical management of the adnexa.

vignette:
A 55-year-old right-handed man with no significant medical history presented with two days of worsening “heaviness” in his right arm. He denied gait difficulty, pain, sensory changes, or cranial symptoms. He had an upper respiratory illness three weeks earlier and denied diarrhea or recent vaccinations. On arrival, blood pressure was 220/139 mm Hg; he was afebrile and alert. Examination showed uniform weakness of the right upper extremity (motor strength 3/5) with 1+ reflexes; left upper extremity and bilateral lower extremities had strength 5/5 with 2+ reflexes. Sensation was intact, cranial nerves were normal, and he walked unassisted. Urine toxicology, head CT, brain MRI with diffusion‐weighted imaging, and cervical‐spine imaging were all unremarkable. He was admitted for observation. On hospital day 2, lumbar puncture showed 1 white blood cell, no red blood cells, and protein 33 mg/dL. Serum assay for botulinum toxin was negative. On hospital day 3, right arm strength declined to 2/5, and new left arm weakness (4/5) appeared; repeat MRI remained normal. On hospital day 4, he was unable to walk unassisted, had complete flaccid paralysis of the right arm, left arm strength 3/5, and areflexia throughout all extremities.

vignette:
A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.

A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presents with severe left knee pain and bilateral genu valgum deformity. She recalls being told she “may have had rickets” at age 9 but was lost to follow-up. • Serum phosphate: low

• Parathyroid hormone: low

vignette:
A 49-year-old woman was referred for surgical management of a presumed large nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma. She reported a 2-year history of chronic bitemporal headache, unexplained easy fatigability, and very slowly progressive diminution of vision. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, visual acuity was decreased bilaterally (worse on the left) with bitemporal homonymous hemianopia. Endocrinological evaluation revealed central hypothyroidism, and levothyroxine replacement was initiated. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a slightly hyperdense large sellar/suprasellar mass extending into both cavernous sinuses with right parasellar extension and bony remodeling of the sella turcica and upper clivus. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 36 × 41 × 50 mm sellar/suprasellar/parasellar mass with heterogeneous low T1 signal, intermediate high T2 signal, small central areas of diffusion restriction on DWI, and mild patchy postcontrast enhancement. The lesion encased the cavernous and clinoid segments of the right internal carotid artery and partially encased the left cavernous segment. The optic nerves and chiasm were elevated and inseparable from the mass, and the pituitary gland and stalk were not visualized.

vignette:
A 34-year-old woman presented with 6 months of progressive left proptosis, with recent ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage after a sudden rise in blood pressure. She had intact ocular motility, a best-corrected visual acuity of 0.9 in the left eye, and normal anterior and posterior segment examinations without optic nerve signs. The right eye was anophthalmic following enucleation in 2010 for a large choroidal melanoma confirmed by histopathology and metastatic workup; she received no adjuvant therapy and was lost to follow-up after 2 years of disease-free status. Orbital CT showed a well-defined isodense intraconal lesion measuring 2.6 × 2.5 × 2.4 mm with intrinsic high-density areas, located inferomedially between the optic nerve and inferior rectus, displacing them and scalloping the lamina papyracea. MRI demonstrated a hyperintense mass on T1-weighted images and hypointense signal on T2-weighted images. General physical examination and systemic metastatic evaluation were negative. An incisional biopsy via anterior inferomedial transconjunctival orbitotomy was planned.

vignette:
A 66-year-old man was referred for recurrent perianal abscesses over 12 months. His history included perianal trauma from sitting on broken glass in childhood; comorbidities were vascular dementia, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and gout. He reported no perianal warts, sexually transmitted diseases, immune deficiency, inflammatory dermatoses, arsenic exposure, or family history of malignancy. Examination revealed a fluctuant left lateral perianal mass without external fistulas. Ultrasound‐guided aspiration yielded 15 cc of purulent fluid; Gram stain and cultures were negative, but cytology showed atypical squamous cells. Postdrainage differential diagnosis included squamous cell carcinoma, cyst, condyloma, or large abscess. Two months later, the mass had enlarged, prompting concern for a fistula. Surgical drainage again yielded purulent fluid without microbial growth. On examination under anesthesia less than one month later, an external sinus tract into the mass was noted but no fistula to the anal canal. It was then decided to excise the mass completely and close the defect primarily.

Mild wheezing was auscultated bilaterally; neurologic and skin findings were normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference: 0–0.3 mg/dL) and a normal white-cell count with a neutrophil count of 3.97 × 10^3/μL. HIV testing was negative. Initial microbiologic studies—including bacterial cultures, acid-fast bacillus smear and culture of sputum, blood cultures (bacterial and fungal), and respiratory viral serologies—were all negative. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated multiple nodules and masses of various sizes in both lung fields, some with cavitation. Chest CT (lung window) showed cavitary and noncavitary nodules and masses with faint surrounding ground-glass opacity (“halo sign”). Cavitary lesions had thick, irregular walls with septa-like structures; on mediastinal windows, one lesion contained a hypoattenuating area. A coronal maximum intensity projection image showed patent vessels within the lesions. A small bilateral pleural effusion was present. 

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titers (both c-ANCA and p-ANCA) were within normal limits. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy revealed diffuse granulomatous inflammation but no organisms. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of a cavitary lesion was performed. Histopathologic analysis showed diffuse necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and fungal elements. Methenamine silver staining revealed yeast-like structures associated with septate hyphae demonstrating acute-angle branching.

An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative.

CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

vignette:
A 40-year-old man presented with 5 days of progressive dyspnea. On day 1 he was short of breath only with uphill walking (MMRC grade 1), by day 2 he was breathless on level ground (grade 2), and by day 4 he was dyspneic at rest (grade 4). He also noted central, nonradiating chest pain with coughing, without positional change. He denied fever, night sweats, cyanosis, grunting, palpitations, or hemoptysis. He had three previous hospital admissions, most recently 4 months earlier for acute severe pancreatitis. He had a 5-year history of local alcohol consumption but had abstained for 6 months. 

On examination, pulse was 116/min, respiratory rate 30/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, temperature 98 °F, and SpO2 95% on 4 L O2 by nasal prong. He had bilateral pitting edema to the knees. Chest inspection showed decreased movement on the left; trachea deviated rightward; decreased fremitus and stony dullness over the entire left hemithorax; and absent breath sounds on the left. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there were no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, WBC 5530/mm3, CRP 73.9 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 145 U/L, serum albumin 3.1 g/dL, serum amylase 486 U/L, and lipase 416 U/L. 

Chest radiograph revealed complete opacification of the left hemithorax with tracheal shift to the right, consistent with massive left pleural effusion. 

Ultrasonography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed a large left pleural effusion with passive basal lung collapse, and showed a normal-sized pancreas with heterogeneous echotexture and a small intrapancreatic collection at the tail. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple non-enhancing cystic areas in the pancreas (largest 23×16 mm in the tail), minimal peripancreatic fat stranding, and no main pancreatic duct dilation or parenchymal calcifications. 

Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded 900 mL of dark brown, turbid fluid. Pleural fluid analysis: protein 3.5 g/dL; LDH 1413 U/L; glucose 98 mg/dL; ADA 31.4 U/L; total cell count 100/mm3 (10% neutrophils, 90% lymphocytes); amylase 11,871 U/L; PCV 0.8%; no malignant cells; culture negative; MTB/RIF PCR negative.

vignette:
A 55-year-old woman presented with generalized gum bleeding and halitosis. Her medical history was noncontributory, and she had undergone orthodontic treatment 18 years earlier. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Intraorally, there was generalized bleeding on probing and clinical attachment loss; radiographs showed generalized alveolar bone loss consistent with stage II, grade II periodontitis. Periapical radiographs of the maxillary central incisors revealed cervical areas of rarefaction. On endodontic evaluation, both central incisors were normal in color, responded normally to cold testing, and were asymptomatic to percussion and palpation. A 5 mm probing depth was recorded on the palatal aspects of both teeth. Two additional periapical radiographs with mesial and distal angulation showed that the lesion’s projection remained in the same position relative to the canal and that the canal outline was undisturbed. Cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated radiolucent resorptive lesions cervically on the palatal aspects of teeth #11 and #21, originating from the external palatal surface and perforating into the pulp space. The diagnosis for both central incisors was asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues and external cervical resorption.

vignette:
A 34-year-old Filipino man presented with a 4-month history of left eye proptosis, diplopia, and chemosis without epistaxis, headache, or nasal obstruction. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a mass at the level of the left middle turbinate extending into the left nasal roof and eroding the upper nasal septum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed mild left proptosis with full extraocular movements, no papilledema, and normal visual acuity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an expansile, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the anterosuperior nasal cavity encroaching on the left orbital cavity, with remodeling of the left medial orbital wall and extension to the level of the cribriform plate, along with retention of secretions in the left frontal sinus. MRI (T1-weighted postcontrast) showed an enhancing mass reaching the nasal vault without dural enhancement or intracranial extension; T2 and non–contrast T1 sequences revealed no intratumoral hemorrhage or cystic change. The patient underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which disclosed a cystic mass occupying the left fronto-ethmoid region with destruction of the anterior skull base and erosion of the left lamina papyracea; the dura was exposed but intact, and no cerebrospinal fluid leak was noted. A routine functional endoscopic sinus surgery was completed after tumor excision.

vignette:
A 41-year-old man presented with a long-standing history of left plantar heel pain. Over two and a half years, he underwent extensive physiotherapy for presumed plantar fasciitis and tight gastrocnemius muscles, treatment with anti-inflammatory and analgesic medications, and two separate surgical releases (endoscopic plantar fascia release and minimally invasive gastrocnemius release) with only temporary relief. On re-presentation, he reported recurrent heel pain upon return to work.

On examination, he walked with an antalgic gait. The gastrocnemius remained tight with a positive Silfverskiöld test, and there was non-specific tenderness over the plantar aspect of the calcaneus at the insertion of the plantar fascia. 

Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and lateral radiographs of the foot demonstrated normal bony relationships with no fractures, lesions, or signs of arthritis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot showed no thickening of the plantar fascia and no signal alteration in adjacent soft tissues or bone marrow. However, MRI revealed a pedunculated bony protrusion arising from the posterolateral plantar aspect of the calcaneus, measuring approximately 1.1 cm × 0.9 cm.

vignette:
A 36-year-old man presented with a two-month history of dull, nonradiating back pain. He denied urinary symptoms, limb weakness, or sensory changes. vignette:
A 44-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 2 days of sharp, stabbing right-sided chest pain (8/10) worsened by exertion and relieved by leaning forward, accompanied by shortness of breath on minimal activity. She also reported chronic right lower-leg swelling and six months of symmetric wrist stiffness that improved during the day. Her history included heavy menstrual bleeding, a miscarriage at age 14, chronic warfarin-refractory deep vein thromboses, and placement of a nonretrievable inferior vena cava filter. She denied fevers, chills, or intravenous drug use.

On examination she was obese and mildly tachypneic, sitting forward. Vital signs: temperature 98.6°F, blood pressure 116/91 mm Hg, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had a malar rash, jugular venous distension, tender anterior chest wall, bibasilar Velcro crackles, and a grade 2/6 pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border that increased with inspiration.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelets 71 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 55 mm/h, CRP 90.9 mg/L, D-dimer 3.7 µg/mL, and prolonged PTT of 49 s with normal PT/INR/fibrinogen. Blood cultures were negative. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated small bilateral pleural effusions and multifocal atelectasis without pulmonary embolism. Lower-extremity duplex ultrasound was negative for DVT. Chest radiograph revealed cardiomegaly, blunting of the right costophrenic angle, and elevated bilateral hemidiaphragms. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 55–60%, moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation, a 1.6 × 0.9 cm tricuspid-valve vegetation, and mild pericardial effusion. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed vegetations on all three tricuspid leaflets.

Based on these findings, rheumatic heart disease and nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis were considered in the differential diagnosis.

vignette:
A 78-year-old woman with a history of two prior catheter ablations for persistent atrial fibrillation—initial pulmonary vein isolation followed six months later by repeat pulmonary vein reisolation, complex fractionated electrogram ablation, and linear lesions across the left atrial roof and mitral isthmus—presented with palpitations. A 12-lead ECG during tachycardia showed an atrial cycle length of 280 ms with positive P waves in leads II, III, aVF, and V₁. An electroanatomic activation map demonstrated counterclockwise propagation around the mitral annulus and left atrial appendage, interrupted by a low-voltage scar at the prior mitral isthmus line. Entrainment pacing revealed postpacing intervals within 20 ms of the tachycardia cycle length at the inferior and lateral mitral annulus and at the left atrial appendage–left pulmonary vein ridge, but a postpacing interval more than 20 ms longer than the cycle length when pacing adjacent to the mitral isthmus scar. These findings suggested an epicardial pathway bypassing the scar. A 2F octapolar catheter was advanced into the vein of Marshall, and recordings showed activation within the vein of Marshall that matched the tachycardia cycle length.

response.rationale: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is the most likely diagnosis given the combination of progressive confusion, multiple occipital lesions with vasogenic edema, and a known risk factor of exposure to pigeons (a source of Toxoplasma gondii). Metastatic brain tumor is a reasonable alternative but is less likely because there is no identified primary malignancy and no systemic abnormalities. Glioblastoma is usually a solitary lesion and less commonly presents with multiple separate enhancing lesions; no prior radiation or genetic predisposition is mentioned.
PML typically occurs in immunocompromised patients, and MRI shows non-enhancing white matter lesions without significant vasogenic edema; also, focal deficits are common, which are absent here.
Primary CNS lymphoma often presents with periventricular enhancing lesions and is frequently associated with immunosuppression; no such risk factor or imaging pattern is present.
SSPE is a childhood/adolescent disease following measles infection; MRI findings are not mass lesions with edema, and the patient's age and exposure history do not fit.
CJD is a rapidly progressive prion disease with characteristic cortical ribboning and basal ganglia changes on MRI, not mass lesions with vasogenic edema; hypertension is unrelated.

vignette:
A 54-year-old woman was brought to the neurosurgical emergency department by her family because of a two-month history of progressive mental confusion with marked worsening over the past two weeks, leading to complete dependence for basic activities of daily living. Her only past medical history was well-controlled hypertension. She had grown up on a farm and had regular contact with various birds, including pigeons. 

On examination, she was normotensive and in poor general condition, able only to obey simple commands. Gait could not be assessed because she was bedbound due to generalized weakness. There were no focal motor deficits, no cranial-nerve abnormalities, and no meningeal signs. Her score on the Karnofsky performance scale was 50. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, performed a few days earlier, revealed two left occipital lesions with surrounding vasogenic edema. She had no other systemic abnormalities. Preoperative laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram, were all within normal limits. 

Given the radiographic appearance and the clinical decline, the decision was made to proceed with neurosurgical resection of the occipital lesions.

vignette:
An 18-year-old woman presented with 2 days of fever and vomiting followed by 1 day of weakness in all four limbs and speech difficulty. Her temperature was 101.4 °F; other vital signs were normal. She was fully conscious (GCS 15). Fundoscopic examination was normal. Neurologically, she had bilateral horizontal gaze palsy with impaired oculocephalic reflexes, bulbar dysarthria, and quadriplegia with bilateral extensor plantar responses; there were no signs of meningeal irritation. Chest, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed anemia, reduced packed cell volume, and thrombocytopenia. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a normal total cell count (all lymphocytes) and mildly elevated protein. Serum dengue NS1 antigen was positive; anti-dengue IgM and IgG were not detected. MRI of the brain demonstrated T1 hypointensity and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the bilateral thalami, pons, medulla, and left cerebellum, with intense diffusion restriction on DWI and central blooming on GRE sequences, producing a “double-doughnut” appearance; there was also an acute infarct in right frontal white matter.

vignette:
A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with a worsening facial rash that began 6 days earlier. It initially appeared as red papules over the left cheek; her pediatrician prescribed acyclovir for presumed eczema herpeticum and instructed her to discontinue all topical products. Over the next 3 days, the rash progressed markedly, and she was brought to the hospital. 

Her medical history was notable only for a nonspecific facial rash of 2 years’ duration on both cheeks, diagnosed as atopic dermatitis and treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily. She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned. She stopped the ointment completely 3 days before presentation. She denied fever, systemic symptoms, or personal or family history of atopy.

On examination, she was afebrile and appeared well. There were confluent erythematous, edematous plaques in the bilateral periorbital areas (left more than right), studded with numerous 2– to 3-mm pustules, some coalescing into “lakes of pus.” A few pustules were also noted in the perioral area. There were no signs of steroid-induced atrophy, such as skin thinning or increased vascular prominence.

vignette:
A 36-year-old woman presented with diffuse abdominal pain and fever. She had a soft, non-tender abdomen. Her white-cell count was 19.3×10^9/L, and C-reactive protein was 103 mg/L. Her medical history included idiopathic urinary retention requiring self-catheterisation, Moyamoya disease, asymptomatic gallstones, livedo reticularis, and peptic ulceration. Over the previous 11 years, she had 13 similar admissions with abdominal pain; on each occasion, inflammatory markers and other blood tests were normal, and imaging (erect chest radiograph or abdominal CT) showed free intraperitoneal air. Each episode resolved rapidly with conservative management, and repeat imaging demonstrated reduction of free air. In 2010, a diagnostic laparoscopy showed no visceral perforation or other pathology. On her current admission, an erect chest radiograph again demonstrated free intraperitoneal air. Two diagnoses were considered: perforated viscus or recurrence of her previous pneumoperitoneum. After discussion, she declined surgical exploration. Conservative management with empirical antibiotics and intravenous fluids was instituted and resulted in rapid reduction of inflammatory markers and the volume of intraperitoneal air.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 15-month history of vaginal bleeding and intermittent sensation of a mass in the vagina. She described bleeding with clots every 1–2 weeks lasting 2–5 days without a separate menstrual cycle; between bleeding episodes she had a watery, nonfoul-smelling vaginal discharge and occasional postcoital bleeding. Her obstetric history included three home vaginal deliveries; she underwent minilaparotomy sterilization 11 years prior and tubal recanalization 5 years ago. Prior evaluations—including coagulation studies, pelvic ultrasonography, and empiric therapy with progesterone, tranexamic acid, and antibiotics—had not alleviated her symptoms.

On examination she appeared pale but hemodynamically stable. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. On bimanual pelvic examination there was a firm, globular 6×4 cm mass within the vaginal canal; a separate cervical os could not be identified and the uterine fundus was not palpable. Active vaginal bleeding was noted. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL with normal platelet count and PT/INR. Pelvic ultrasonography—performed multiple times, including in the preoperative area—was reported as normal and was unable to clarify the origin of the mass. Magnetic resonance imaging was not available. After resuscitation with intravenous fluids and two units of whole blood, she was scheduled for emergency surgical management.

vignette:
A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.

vignette:
A 17-year-old boy presented on the fourth day of an acute febrile illness. He reported fever and severe myalgia for 4 days, productive cough with yellow sputum but no hemoptysis, and 3 days of watery diarrhea. On the day of transfer, he developed oliguria and noted red-colored urine. He denied trauma, exertion, medication ingestion, or freshwater exposures.

On examination, temperature 38.4 °C, pulse 102 bpm, blood pressure 100/80 mm Hg, GCS 15. He appeared unwell, with generalized muscle tenderness and restricted movement due to pain. Chest auscultation was clear bilaterally; the abdomen revealed right hypochondrial tenderness without hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic exam was normal.

Laboratory studies showed reduced ionized calcium 8.16 mg/dL, elevated phosphate 5.4 mg/dL, and normal magnesium. Initial abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. He was admitted to the ICU and treated with acetaminophen and empiric intravenous cefotaxime and clarithromycin. Over the next ten hours he developed sinus tachycardia up to 150–195 bpm and hypotension requiring fluid adjustments guided by central venous pressure and vasopressors. Chest radiograph and echocardiogram were unremarkable. A repeat abdominal ultrasound remained normal. Urinalysis showed no red cells, mild proteinuria, and 6–8 pus cells per high-power field. Serum creatine phosphokinase was markedly elevated at over 90,000 U/L.

vignette:
A 41-year-old woman with a 3-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presented with the sudden onset of visual disturbances. At the time of her SSc diagnosis, she had skin sclerosis of the fingers, hands, forearms, and face, Raynaud’s phenomenon with digital ulcers, multiple facial telangiectasias, esophageal reflux, and interstitial lung disease. Nail-fold capillaroscopy showed capillary loss with dilatation and microhemorrhages. A forearm skin biopsy demonstrated increased dermal collagen and superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. Laboratory studies revealed a positive antinuclear antibody titer (>1:320) with a nucleolar pattern, negative anti-centromere antibody, and negative anti-Scl-70 antibody. She was treated with bosentan and aspirin, with stable pulmonary findings over two years.

Seven days before transfer, she was admitted elsewhere for fever over 38°C and headache. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 161.6 mg/dL, glucose 39 mg/dL, red blood cells 0 /mm3, and white blood cells 459 /mm3 (88% polymorphonuclear cells). Serum C-reactive protein was 10.6 mg/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 82 mm/h. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T2 hyperintense lesions in the frontal, left parietal, and left occipital lobes with leptomeningeal enhancement. Empirical ceftriaxone and vancomycin were initiated. After four days, she developed visual disturbances; repeat MRI showed increased size and number of multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions along both cerebral hemispheres and midbrain, including a 4.5-cm lesion in the right posterior lobe. Tests of CSF—including Gram stain and culture, PCR for herpes simplex virus and enteroviruses, cryptococcal antigen, and fungal cultures—were negative. She was then referred to our hospital.

On arrival, she could only count fingers at close range and also reported headache, dizziness, fever, myalgia, polyarthralgia, and bilateral foot tingling. Blood pressure was 192/103 mmHg, heart rate 48 beats/min, and temperature 37.3°C. Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia. Neurologic examination revealed drowsiness, neck stiffness, symmetrical proximal and distal weakness (muscle strength 4/5), paresthesia in both feet, brisk biceps reflexes, absent patellar reflexes, and bilaterally positive Babinski signs. A 4 × 5 cm ulcer was noted over the right lateral malleolus; there was no synovitis. The white-cell count was 14,090 /mm3, C-reactive protein was 3.09 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 56 mm/h. She continued antibiotics, and intravenous acyclovir, nicardipine, mannitol, and dexamethasone were added. Blood pressure stabilized within six hours, but her visual impairment worsened, and she developed left-sided weakness and new Raynaud’s phenomenon in her fingers. Emergent cerebral angiography revealed diffuse stenosis and a beaded pattern of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries and their branches, along with diffuse luminal narrowing and dysplastic changes in the right distal vertebral artery and basilar trunk, consistent with cerebral angiitis.

vignette:
A 63-year-old white man presented with a 3-week history of redness of the left eye and extensive bilateral lymphadenopathy. He reported blurred vision and loss of vision in the left lower quadrant, with supraorbital pain in both eyes, all worsening over 3 weeks. His lymph nodes (preauricular, submandibular, cervical, supraclavicular, and axillary) had progressively enlarged. He denied fever, chills, weight loss, rash, or joint pains, but noted several weeks of malaise.

Initial treatment for presumed viral and bacterial conjunctivitis included erythromycin ointment three times daily for 2 weeks, followed by topical prednisolone, tobramycin/dexamethasone ointment, and cyclopentolate without improvement. On presentation, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/125 in the left. Intraocular pressure was 11 mm Hg in the right eye and 32 mm Hg in the left. Slit-lamp examination showed 1+ cell in the right eye, 4+ cell in the left, and a gelatinous layered hypopyon with red-blood-cell layering in both eyes, consistent with a hemorrhagic hypopyon. Dilated exam revealed 1+ vitreous haze and optic-nerve pallor in the left eye; the right eye was unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed no retinal detachment or masses.

He was diagnosed with panuveitis, with malignancy or infection strongly suspected. An anterior chamber paracentesis of the left eye yielded only acellular, dense, proteinaceous material.

vignette:

A 51-year-old man presented with a gradually enlarging mass in his left thigh, first noted 10 years previously and painful for the past 6 months. vignette:
A 62-year-old man was admitted on June 25, 2021, with a 20-day history of episodic slurred speech that had worsened over the previous 9 days. Initially, episodes lasted about 10 minutes without loss of consciousness, headache, dizziness, diplopia, dysphagia, or limb weakness; by presentation, they occurred 2–3 times daily lasting about 30 minutes. His medical history included hypertension (>20 years), diabetes mellitus (8 years), and coronary heart disease (8 years); he was blind bilaterally after retinal detachment in adolescence. He denied smoking and alcohol use. On examination, temperature was 36.5°C, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 17/min, and blood pressure 144/86 mmHg. Cranial nerve exam showed dysarthria and midline tongue extension; limb strength was 5/5 with normal tone; Babinski and other reflexes were normal; he had no light perception with irregular pupils and absent light reflexes. Routine blood tests, coagulation studies, rheumatologic panels, thyroid function, tumor markers, liver and kidney function, and electrolytes were all normal. Brain MRI and susceptibility-weighted imaging were unremarkable; MRA showed mild cerebral arteriosclerosis; carotid MRA showed carotid arteriosclerosis with limited stenosis of the intracranial left vertebral artery; transcranial Doppler was normal. The initial diagnosis was transient ischemic attack of the vertebrobasilar system. On review, symptoms did not improve with rest; a fatigue test and a neostigmine test were both negative.

There was also adenoid hypertrophy and mild sinus mucosal thickening.

vignette:
An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

vignette:
A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. He reported ingestion and insufflation of “bath salts,” a history later confirmed by his family. He denied other medications or supplements and had no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 107°F, blood pressure 91/52 mm Hg, and pulse 93/min. He was confused and intermittently agitated, with pupils 3 mm and equal. Cardiovascular exam showed weak peripheral pulses without jugular venous distention or murmurs; lungs were clear; abdomen was soft; no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Urine toxicology detected only lorazepam and cotinine but was negative for over 80 other substances, including cannabinoids, cocaine, ecstasy, ephedrine, lysergide, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, oxycodone, and phencyclidine.

Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. Urine output was 4200 mL over the first 24 hours, then declined to 825 mL and 150 mL over subsequent 24-hour periods. He was started on daily hemodialysis for volume control and solute clearance.

vignette:
A 17-year-old nulliparous female presented with a two-year history of gradually progressive abdominal distension. She initially sought evaluation for bloating but was advised to diet for presumed weight gain. She denied pain, vaginal bleeding, or systemic symptoms. There was no personal or family history of cancer. On examination, her BMI was 20.5 kg/m2, blood pressure 125/85 mmHg, pulse 89/min, and SpO2 95% on room air. The abdomen was markedly distended with a palpable mass rising approximately 3 cm above the umbilicus. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an 18 cm diameter ovarian tumor. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL with a microcytic profile (MCV 73.2 fL); APTT, INR, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine were normal. Tumor markers included HE4 69.1 pmol/L (N ≤ 60.5), LDH 202 U/L (N ≤ 48.5), with alpha-fetoprotein 4.54 ng/mL (N ≤ 5.8), CA-125 23.1 U/mL (N ≤ 35), and β-hCG <0.2 mIU/mL all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, fluid-filled lesion measuring 19.3 × 6.2 × 21 cm, located in the pelvis and mid-abdomen, displacing the uterus and compressing the aorta and inferior vena cava. The lesion appeared unilocular with a 1.5 mm wall and no septations or solid components, and was suggestive of an ovarian origin.
