vignette:
A 50-year-old man with known neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple cutaneous neurofibromas, and no history of smoking, was admitted for recurrent urinary retention and sepsis. A transurethral resection of the prostate revealed fibroleiomyomatous hyperplasia, but urinary function did not improve. Laboratory studies and a CT scan showed diffuse irregular polypoid thickening of the entire bladder wall without a discrete mass. Because of compromised bladder function, the patient underwent cystoprostatectomy. 

On gross examination, the bladder wall was diffusely thickened, firm, and gray–white, with near–complete loss of the detrusor muscle. Histologic evaluation revealed in the superficial wall a diffuse bland spindle cell proliferation with comma-shaped nuclei and a collagenous matrix. In the deeper wall, there was a dense, perivascular spindle cell proliferation with prominent cytological atypia, frequent mitoses, and an infiltrative growth pattern. The tumor was in close contact with peripheral nerves. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for S100, p16, neurofilaments, and CD56, and negative for pan-cytokeratin, EMA, MDM2, p63, ALK, CD117, DOG1, myogenin, desmin, and smooth muscle actin.

vignette:
A 57-year-old man with stage cS4a mantle cell lymphoma in complete remission after induction chemoimmunotherapy presented in August 2018 with painful swelling of the calves. There was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or soft-tissue infection. He reported a brief gastroenteritis episode at that time. Diuretics gave transient relief, but over weeks the swelling spread to the upper extremities and trunk muscles. Systemic steroids and a short discontinuation of ibrutinib had no effect.

By November 2018, calf swelling worsened; examination was notable only for one slightly enlarged right inguinal lymph node. Laboratory tests showed elevated LDH and CK, with negative autoimmune serology. Analgesics provided minimal benefit. In January 2019, CT scan showed no lymphoma relapse but diffuse subcutaneous edema. The patient’s condition deteriorated, and he was hospitalized with generalized muscle pain, ECOG performance status 3, massive edema (especially of the lower extremities), and extreme muscle tenderness. Neurologic exam showed only weak symmetric fist closure and shoulder lift; no focal deficits.

Initial evaluations were consistent with myositis of unknown cause. Ibrutinib and rituximab were discontinued. Laboratory testing revealed elevated CRP, transaminases, CK, troponin I, myoglobin, and LDH, with reduced plasma protein, albumin, and IgG; leukocyte count was elevated. MRI of the thighs showed diffuse intramuscular and extramuscular edema. Muscle biopsy demonstrated interstitial and perivascular T-cell and macrophage infiltrates with variation in fiber size, centrally located nuclei, necrosis, and regeneration. The patient developed acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Troponin I rose further; ECG revealed a new right bundle branch block and repolarization disturbances, and he developed atrial fibrillation. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocarditis. Over the next days, increasing somnolence and personality changes were noted. Brain MRI was unremarkable, but spinal MRI demonstrated a hyperintense lesion concerning for myelitis. CSF analysis showed leukocyte count 329/μl, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, and protein 79.6 mg/dl.

vignette:
A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

vignette:
A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

vignette:
A 74-year-old right-handed woman was brought to the psychiatry clinic with a 5-month history of abrupt onset of disorganized speech, severe anxiety, and self-harm behaviors that began after a family trip. Her speech was rapid, fluent, and nonsensical—exemplified by the phrase “Our neighbor has gone to the cobbler to buy Ghormeh Sabzi”—consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. Over the ensuing months, she developed agitation, persecutory delusions, visual and auditory hallucinations, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a persistent urge to flee her home.

Her psychiatric history included a 10-year history of depression treated with sertraline. There was no prior cognitive impairment or neurological disease. On examination, she was disoriented to time, demonstrated anomia, and had marked perseveration on the Clock Drawing Test, impaired performance on Luria’s three-step test, and defective crossed-pentagon drawing. Cognitive testing revealed an MMSE score of 2/30 and an ACE-R score of 2/100, likely confounded by comprehension deficits.

An initial brain MRI performed 2 months after symptom onset was reported as normal. She was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and started on memantine and quetiapine, without clinical improvement. Because of the acute presentation and prominent frontal and temporal features, she was referred to neurology for further assessment.

vignette:
A 41-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 2-year history of progressively worsening fever, weight loss, night sweats, and a dry cough. He also reported chronic lower back pain without neurologic deficits and a painful nonhealing ulcer on his right hallux. He had two sputum GeneXpert tests at local clinics, both negative. vignette:
A 69-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of a painless, firm area of induration and mild erythema below her left lower eyelid. Her history included chronic scleritis treated successfully with NSAIDs, left levator resection for ptosis, and a dacryocystorhinostomy one month before the onset of the lesion. The final histopathology showed granulomatous inflammation with central necrobiosis, extensive Alcian-Blue positive mucin, and scattered multinucleated giant cells. vignette:
A 20-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, and melena. She had no significant past medical history and no family history of cancer. On examination, she had mild abdominal tenderness; gynecological examination was normal. Laboratory studies revealed iron-deficiency anemia; white blood cell and platelet counts were normal. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance enterography demonstrated a focal segment of small-bowel wall thickening measuring 15 mm by 2 mm. An exploratory laparotomy revealed an exophytic ileal mass with mesenteric lymphadenopathy but no peritoneal or hepatic metastases. A wide segmental resection was performed without complication.

Gross examination showed a 30 mm by 25 mm polypoid, tan-white, lobulated mass arising from the small-intestinal wall. Microscopically, the lesion was a transmural, infiltrative proliferation of uniform epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in nested and fascicular patterns, with variable eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, round to oval vesicular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and up to 10 mitoses per 10 high-power fields; there was mucosal ulceration but no melanin pigment, lymphovascular invasion, or perineural invasion, and three mesenteric lymph nodes were negative for tumor.

Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse, strong positivity for S100 protein and SOX10; HMB45 and Melan A were negative. There was patchy synaptophysin expression. CD117, DOG1, cytokeratin, CD34, smooth muscle actin, desmin, chromogranin, and CD56 were all negative.

A 69-year-old Japanese man presented with pain and a 10-mm polypoid mass on the left lower gingiva. An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture.

Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted.  
An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

vignette:
A 74-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer and a known left upper lobe lung mass presented with four weeks of progressive vertigo, described as the sensation that “the floor was wobbling” and “the room was swaying,” leading to difficulty ambulating. Two days prior, he was evaluated at an outside emergency department, tested positive for adenovirus, and was discharged after supportive treatment without symptom relief.

His oncology history included stage III prostate adenocarcinoma treated with prostatectomy and radiation in 2013, followed by detection of bilateral lung nodules and sclerotic bone lesions in 2016, and a 2020 biopsy of a left upper lobe lesion confirming mismatch repair deficient, androgen receptor–positive metastatic prostate cancer treated with enzalutamide, then abiraterone acetate and prednisone, and palliative radiation.

On presentation, vital signs were: temperature 37°C, heart rate 90 beats/min, blood pressure 164/81 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed no focal motor or sensory deficits; intact coordination on dysdiadochokinesia, finger-to-nose, and heel-to-shin testing; an intact gait despite dizziness; and a positive right-sided Dix–Hallpike maneuver with horizontal nystagmus.

Noncontrast head CT showed a 3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema causing mild partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and left quadrigeminal cistern. The patient received dexamethasone. MRI of the brain demonstrated a cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect; no other intra-axial lesions were identified. Cerebral angiography revealed no abnormal hyperemia at the site of the lesion.

Dedicated MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 was negative. MRI of the hips and pelvis showed bilateral thigh intramuscular edema with enhancement. vignette:
A 32-year-old man presented with a six-year history of a painless swelling in the left supraclavicular region that had gradually enlarged from the size of an almond to that of a lime. He reported no history of trauma, fever, or systemic illness, and no weakness, numbness, or loss of function in the upper limb. On examination, there was a 4.0-cm diameter, round, firm, non-tender mass in the left supraclavicular area that was mobile in the medio-lateral direction. An ultrasound showed a superficial heterogeneous round cystic mass measuring 47 × 33 mm lateral to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with well-defined smooth margins and multiple intralesional septa; its lower border lay adjacent to the subclavian artery and its medial border abutted the carotid artery and external jugular vein. The ultrasound was interpreted as a branchial cleft cyst with an atypical location. Fine needle aspiration was performed, and the cystogram findings corroborated this diagnosis. The patient was scheduled for surgical excision of the suspected branchial cleft cyst.

vignette:
A 28-year-old man with a history of migraine disorder presented with several months of pain and swelling in the right mastoid area, with a recent subjective enlargement of the mass and increased pain. vignette:
A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. On examination, the left breast had a 4 × 4 cm hard lump in the lower inner quadrant fixed to the chest wall; the right breast had a firm, mobile 1 × 1 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant. MRI showed a 3.8 × 3.5 cm irregular spiculated mass in the left breast suspicious for malignancy and a 2.3 × 1.5 cm well-defined lesion in the right breast with a type 1 contrast enhancement pattern (< 6% probability of malignancy) and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound and bone scan were negative for metastases. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left breast lump revealed poorly cohesive clusters of ductal cells with pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli; myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei were absent. FNAC of the left axillary lymph node showed similar malignant cells. FNAC of the right breast lump showed three-dimensional clusters of hyperchromatic cells with prominent nucleoli and scattered pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures admixed with benign ductal cells and myoepithelial cells; a few bare nuclei were seen. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

A 67‐year‐old man with a 3‐year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, glimepiride, and a prior percutaneous coronary intervention for acute myocardial infarction 2 months earlier was referred for treatment of newly diagnosed extensive ulcerative colitis. On admission for a 2‐week educational trial of a plant‐based diet, his body weight was 69 kg and physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed normal white‐cell count, bilirubin, and liver function tests. Ten days after admission, plasma glucose rose from 258 mg/dL to 449 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c increased from 7.3% to 8.0%. Urinalysis showed no proteinuria but microalbuminuria of 50.7 mg/day. Anti–glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies were negative. Both serum amylase and lipase were elevated. Contrast‐enhanced CT and MR cholangiopancreatography demonstrated swelling of the pancreas with a peripheral rim and slight narrowing of the main pancreatic duct. Serum IgG4 was 36.0 mg/dL (reference range, 4.5–117 mg/dL).

She was referred for hypertensive retinopathy evaluation, where her blood pressure measured 220/130 mmHg and she had cotton-wool spots on funduscopic exam. In the emergency department, her systolic pressure reached 230 mmHg. On examination, jugular venous pressure was 14 cm above the sternal angle; heart sounds were distant without pulsus paradoxus; lungs were clear; and there was no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL (baseline 10 g/dL), creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 11 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 110 mm/hr. Chest radiography demonstrated a markedly enlarged cardiac silhouette with mild pulmonary congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large circumferential pericardial effusion (2.24 cm) with early right ventricular diastolic collapse, respirophasic mitral inflow variation, and a dilated inferior vena cava. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest and cardiac MRI showed no pericardial or pleural thickening, masses, or aortic dissection. She underwent pericardiocentesis yielding 1160 mL of straw-colored fluid. A rheumatologic workup revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:640, positive anti-Smith antibodies, and low complement levels (C3, C4). High-dose intravenous steroids were administered, and a repeat echocardiogram two days later showed reduction of the effusion. Pericardial fluid cytology showed few reactive mesothelial cells and a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate; bacterial, viral, and fungal studies were negative. Immunohistochemical staining of the fluid was positive for calretinin and weakly positive for CK5/6 and MOC31.

vignette:
A 74-year-old Spanish-speaking man visiting the United States from Honduras presented with a 2-month history of postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, night sweats, early satiety, and a 10-kg weight loss. One week earlier, an abdominal and pelvic CT scan had shown distal ileitis, and he had received a course of antibiotics without improvement. On re-presentation, he reported worsening symptoms and difficulty tolerating oral intake. He denied hematochezia, diarrhea, or fevers. His medical history was notable for prior appendectomy and recently treated helminth infection.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. There was no abdominal tenderness or palpable masses, and no evidence of perianal disease. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/hr, a C-reactive protein level of 35 mg/L, and a fecal calprotectin of 94 μg/mg. Stool studies were negative for enteric pathogens. Repeat CT imaging demonstrated persistent distal ileitis.

Ileocolonoscopy revealed a normal terminal ileum, but a nontraversable distal ileal stricture, cecal ulcers, and patchy loss of vascularity throughout the colon. Segmental biopsies of the ileum and colon were obtained. QuantiFERON-TB Gold was positive. Hepatitis B serologies showed a reactive core total antibody, a reactive e antigen, negative surface antigen, and undetectable HBV DNA. He was started on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis.

vignette:
A 30-year-old Asian man presented with a 6-month history of recurrent pain localized to the lateral side of his left knee. On examination, there was slight tenderness and swelling over the lateral joint line without other abnormalities. Plain radiographs were unremarkable, and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. MRI demonstrated a 1.5 cm intra-articular space-occupying lesion invading the tibial plateau. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was homogeneous and isointense to muscle; on T2-weighted images, it appeared heterogeneous with internal specks and was unremarkable on fat-saturated T2 sequences. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed enhancement confined to the peripheral rim of the mass, with no satellite lesions identified.

vignette:
A 45-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a slowly growing, dull, intermittent swelling and discomfort in the right upper vestibule. She reported fluctuations in pain intensity and a sensation of heaviness in the area. On examination, teeth #15 and #16 were grossly carious, and there was a firm, mildly tender diffuse swelling of the adjacent vestibular mucosa. There was no tenderness on percussion of the involved teeth. Panoramic radiography demonstrated a mild periapical radiolucency at the affected root apices. A provisional diagnosis of a periapical abscess was made, and extraction of the carious teeth with socket curettage was planned. Preoperative blood tests (CBC, hemoglobin, blood sugar, bleeding and clotting times) were within normal limits. Under local anesthesia, the teeth were extracted, and curettage yielded a gelatinous, soft, mushy tissue, which was sent for histopathological examination with a provisional diagnosis of periapical granuloma.

vignette:
A 33-year-old Hispanic man with no known past medical history presented with a 1½-week history of headache and blurred vision. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.7-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe with mass effect. He underwent craniotomy with biopsy and resection. Postoperatively, he was found to have HIV infection with a CD4 count <20 cells/µL and an HIV viral load of 191 000 copies/mL. Serum toxoplasma IgG was elevated, and CSF studies showed 48 cells/µL (97% lymphocytes) with positive toxoplasma IgG and DNA-PCR for Toxoplasma gondii (286 copies/mL). Other CSF studies, including fungal cultures, cryptococcal antigen, and AFB smear/culture, were negative. Histopathologic examination of the brain tissue revealed bradyzoites and tachyzoites. He was treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and started on antiretroviral therapy; empiric antibiotics for bacterial abscess were discontinued.

Two weeks after discharge, he returned with fever to 39.6 °C, generalized weakness, and a 1-day history of productive cough. Chest radiograph showed a new left upper lobe opacification with diffuse reticulonodular interstitial prominence. CT scan of the chest confirmed extensive reticulonodular interstitial infiltrates with focal consolidation in the left upper lobe. He was started on vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and fluconazole and placed on airborne precautions. His respiratory status worsened, and intubation was planned pending further diagnostic evaluation.

vignette:
A 60‐year‐old tailor with no significant medical history presented with a 3‐year history of macerated skin between his toes. He complained of a painful, fissured ulcer at the base of the fourth interdigital space of the right foot, which had been progressively enlarging over the past 18 months. He had received multiple antifungal regimens—including topical sertaconazole for 6 weeks and oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 6 weeks—without improvement. On examination, there was a verrucous, infected ulceration with infiltrated, hyperkeratotic edges and a whitish, fissured base measuring 3 cm in diameter, extending onto the dorsum of the foot. Dermoscopy revealed unstructured whitish areas and hyperkeratosis. Popliteal and inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

vignette:
A 47-year-old man was referred for mechanical circulatory support for severe cardiogenic shock with multiorgan failure of unknown cause. One day earlier, he had undergone excision of a benign thyroglossal duct cyst, during which he experienced recurrent hypertensive episodes. After extubation, he developed profound hypotension and pulmonary oedema. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severely impaired left ventricular (LV) systolic function. Coronary angiography revealed no evidence of relevant coronary artery disease, and toxicological screening was negative. His medical history included chronic polyarthritis and treated arterial hypertension.

On transfer, he was invasively ventilated (PaO2/FiO2 30 mmHg), receiving norepinephrine at 2.5 µg/kg/min. Blood pressure was 75/49 mmHg, heart rate 180 b.p.m., with bilateral rales and basal dullness on chest percussion. He experienced pulseless electrical activity requiring 5 minutes of resuscitation. Bedside echocardiography demonstrated akinesia of all basal and mid LV segments with preserved apical contraction (left ventricular ejection fraction, 15%); right ventricular function was preserved (TAPSE 17 mm). On the basis of these findings, reverse takotsubo cardiomyopathy was suspected. A percutaneous LV assist device (Impella CP®) was implanted immediately. Endomyocardial biopsy revealed moderate chronically active myocarditis with diffuse interstitial remodelling, and PCR testing showed no evidence of acute or persistent myocardial infection.

vignette:
A 2-month-old full-term female with known complex congenital heart disease (single ventricle defect, double-outlet right ventricle with D-transposition of the great arteries, and an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with left superior vena cava) was admitted for evaluation of occasional cyanosis. The team planned a pulmonary artery banding, but during the procedure the patient became hemodynamically unstable and suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest requiring cardiac massage, so the operation was aborted. To gather hemodynamic data, cardiac catheterization was performed via the left femoral artery, with the catheter tip in the single ventricle, using serial doses of nonionic iodinated contrast (Iopromide) totaling 3 mL/kg over 30 minutes. A noncontrast head CT obtained after this first seizure showed a slight diffuse increase in cortical density predominantly in the right frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes and, to a lesser extent, in the left parietal and occipital lobes; there was no mass effect, hemorrhage, or other intracranial abnormality.

vignette:
A 38-year-old woman presented with 4 months of progressively worsening symmetric pain in the small joints of her hands, wrists, knees, and ankles. She reported early morning stiffness lasting 2 hours daily and severe fatigue throughout the day. One month before presentation, she had a mild COVID-19 infection confirmed by SARS-CoV-2 PCR; symptoms were limited to fever, chills, and a non-oxygen-requiring cough. She had not been vaccinated against COVID-19 at that time. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, rash, or appetite changes since recovering. There were no recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections and no history of psoriasis or uveitis. She is a non-smoker, does not drink alcohol, and has no recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 13 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein of 4.3 mg/L (both within normal limits). Immunologic testing revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:640, negative extractable nuclear antigen and double-stranded DNA antibodies, a rheumatoid factor of 62.29 IU/mL (normal <20 IU/mL), and an anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody of 237.39 units (normal <20 units). Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Radiographs of the hands, knees, ankles, and feet were unremarkable. Hand ultrasound showed no joint erosion. MRI of the hands demonstrated synovitis of the bilateral distal radioulnar joints and the left second metacarpophalangeal joint, with tenosynovitis around the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon; no osseous destruction was identified.

vignette:
A 6-year-old girl presented with a 1-week history of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain that was worse when supine, associated with orthopnea, mild agitation, and fever. Her parents also reported intermittent fever over the preceding 3 months. There was no significant past medical history and no known contact with COVID-19 patients. Abdominal examination showed hepatomegaly.

- Chest radiograph: mediastinal widening  
- ECG: sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRS and electrical alternans  
- Laboratory studies: WBC 11.4×10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, platelets 565×10^9/L, LDH 1061 U/L, CRP 66 mg/L, ESR 57 mm/h; electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, troponin I, and COVID-19 PCR were unremarkable.

Further evaluation with transthoracic echocardiography showed a large pericardial effusion without signs of tamponade. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT revealed an anterior mediastinal mass accompanied by moderate pleural and pericardial effusions.

vignette:
A 74-year-old Caucasian woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (diagnosed in 2006, complex karyotype with TP53 mutation and trisomy 12) was receiving zanubrutinib and subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement for hypogammaglobulinemia. In May 2022 she was hospitalized for pulmonary sepsis, treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and caspofungin, with resolution. One month later, she developed grade 4 neutropenia (<500/μL) for over 15 days and a febrile peak. Starting 15 June, tender, warm, erythematous nodular skin lesions appeared on the lower limbs and then the upper limbs; the lesions progressed to central ulceration with a necrotic core. 

On 25 June, zanubrutinib was discontinued and oral itraconazole was begun after a 5 mm punch biopsy of a left-thigh lesion. Histopathological examination (HE, Giemsa, GMS, PAS, and Gram stains) showed severe diffuse lympho-monocytic inflammation with minimal necrosis, angioinvasive microbial structures, thrombosed small vessels, and sparse hyphal mats with sporangial-type cells. Within vessels, thin-walled (5–15 μm), pauciseptate hyphae with minimal branching were seen, along with numerous thick-walled ovoid sporangia (5–20 μm) that stained strongly with PAS, GMS, and Giemsa. Only a presumptive diagnosis of deep cutaneous fungal infection was made at this time.

vignette:
A 45-year-old woman was admitted to an acute psychiatric hospital with depressed mood, suicidal ideation, and auditory hallucinations. She had been discharged five days earlier from another facility and had 18 emergency department visits in the prior year. Her psychiatric history included benzodiazepine use disorder, opiate use disorder, borderline personality disorder, and major depressive disorder. Home medications were clonazepam, clonidine, buprenorphine–naloxone, fluoxetine, gabapentin, and trazodone. She was unemployed, homeless, and without family support.

During the admission, she exhibited:
- Catatonia-like signs: flat affect with psychomotor retardation and fluctuating mutism; complete lack of social contact; twitching, eye grimacing, and shoulder shrugging; posturing and immobility; diaphoresis.
- Psychotic signs: mouthing words and seemingly responding to internal stimuli; thought blocking; reported auditory hallucinations.
- Seizure-like behavior: episodes of head jerking with eye fluttering without tongue biting; remained conversant; benign neurologic examination.

Clues suggesting volitional behavior included selective acceptance of benzodiazepines and gabapentin while refusing other medications, eating all meals despite “stupor,” abruptly lapsing into and out of catatonia-like and psychotic behaviors depending on the topic of conversation, purposeful movements to obtain lorazepam after seizures, and evidence of self‐induced urinary incontinence during one episode.

A regional catatonia specialist evaluated her and noted that she was unlikely to have catatonia. Repeated lorazepam challenge tests had limited effect on her behaviors and appeared to reinforce them.

vignette:
A male newborn was referred at 1 day of age for cyanosis; oxygen saturation (SaO2) was 80% in room air. Laboratory findings showed a hematocrit of 47.8% and a platelet count of 103 000/mm3; other values were normal and there were no signs of infection. Echocardiography revealed pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus. A prostaglandin infusion was started, raising SaO2 to 90–95%. On day 11, he underwent a systemic‐to‐pulmonary shunt operation with graft placement and PDA division. Preoperative values on day 10 were hematocrit 38.9%, platelet count 173 000/mm3, and SaO2 95% on prostaglandin. Postoperatively, hematocrit was 52.1% and platelet count was 58 000/mm3; platelet count then increased without transfusion. By postoperative day 6, he was extubated with SaO2 80–85%, hematocrit 41.1%, and platelet count 123 000/mm3. He was discharged on postoperative day 13 with SaO2 85–87%, hematocrit 33.4%, and platelet count 225 000/mm3.

At 10 months of age, he was admitted for a Rastelli operation. His SaO2 was 80%; hematocrit was 49.1% and platelet count was 68 000/mm3. He had no bleeding history or medications. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and INR were normal; peripheral smear was unremarkable. Antiplatelet antibodies and platelet‐associated immunoglobulins were negative; antinuclear and anti–double‐stranded DNA antibodies were normal. Platelet aggregation time was 127 s (reference, 61–110 s). Viral and bacterial studies were insignificant. The pediatrician made a provisional diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia and administered intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg) the day before surgery. On the day of operation, hematocrit was 42.6% and platelet count was 77 000/mm3.

vignette:
A man in his 50s with a 12-year history of recurrent follicular lymphoma presented with a subacute, multifocal, pruritic, painful eruption that began on the abdomen and then involved the scalp, groin, and extremities. He denied fevers, chills, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. His medications included oxycodone, duvelisib (a PI3K inhibitor), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, all started 14 months earlier for lymphoma management. On examination, there were well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the abdomen, axillae, and inguinal folds; scattered erythematous scaly papules and plaques on the scalp, extremities, and hands; and confluent erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques with plate-like scales on the plantar feet. Two skin biopsies (abdomen and left foot) showed parakeratosis with collections of neutrophils, hypogranulosis, regular epidermal hyperplasia with elongated rete ridges, thin suprapapillary plates, dilated papillary dermal vessels, and dermal eosinophils, findings consistent with a psoriasiform drug reaction.

vignette:
A 70-year-old Japanese man presented with dysphagia and was diagnosed with T3N0M0 esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.6%), percutaneous coronary intervention, and radiotherapy for laryngeal cancer. He underwent two courses of 5-fluorouracil/docetaxel/cisplatin and then thoracoscopic esophagectomy with retrosternal gastric tube reconstruction and cervical esophagogastrostomy.

On postoperative day 4, cervical wound erythema with pus and saliva discharge appeared; drainage and intravenous tazobactam/piperacillin were initiated. Despite nutritional support and improved albumin levels, a refractory anastomotic fistula persisted, and Enterobacter cloacae was cultured from the wound. On day 60, salvage reconstruction with a free jejunal autograft and pectoralis major muscle flap coverage was performed.

Fifteen days after reconstruction, he developed worsening low back pain and fever (38.2 °C). Examination revealed lumbar spinal tenderness and bilateral leg weakness without sensory loss. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9200/µL and C-reactive protein of 9.86 mg/dL. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Blood cultures grew Enterobacter cloacae. MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated decreased T1 signal and increased T2 and STIR signal at L4–L5.

response.rationale: Schwannoma is the classic nerve sheath tumor presenting as a well-defined, encapsulated mass along a nerve, causing compressive symptoms (positive Phalen's and Durkan's) and exhibiting the characteristic target sign on contrast-enhanced MRI. The other candidates either lack the target sign (e.g., giant cell tumor, synovial sarcoma, lipoma) or are less likely to cause median nerve compression with this imaging pattern (e.g., ganglion cyst, glomus tumor). Targetoid hemosiderotic hemangioma can show a target sign but is not typically associated with nerve compression.

rejected.why: Target sign is present, but median nerve compression is not a typical feature; vascular lesions are less likely to cause compressive neuropathy.
Nodular tenosynovitis may cause compression but does not classically show a biphasic target sign on contrast-enhanced MRI.
Ganglion cysts are cystic and do not show solid biphasic enhancement; the target sign is not characteristic.
Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath is common on the wrist but typically shows hypointense signal on MRI, not a target enhancement pattern.
Synovial sarcoma is malignant, often ill-defined, and does not present with a target sign; the well-encapsulated nature and chronic course are atypical.
Glomus tumors are usually subungual, intensely painful, and not associated with median nerve compression at the wrist.
Lipomas are fatty and do not enhance in a biphasic target pattern; they are typically non-compressive unless very large.

vignette:
A two-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of progressive, bilateral, painless swelling of the jaws over several months. On examination, he had symmetrical enlargement of the mandible and maxilla with intact, bluish-gray oral mucosa. Vital signs were normal, there was no lymphadenopathy, and routine hematologic tests were unremarkable. Panoramic radiography revealed well-defined, multilocular radiolucent areas involving the mandibular bodies, angles, ascending rami, and the maxillary tuberosities. Computed tomography of the jaws showed bilateral, expansile, multilocular lesions with thinning of the cortical plates of the maxilla and mandible, mild anterior displacement of an unerupted first molar, and no cortical breaches or soft-tissue extension.

vignette:
A 71-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease presented with a 2-month history of intermittent painless hematuria with passage of clots. She denied dysuria, frequency, or other lower urinary tract symptoms, and there was no family history of malignancy. On examination, vital signs and abdominal and pelvic exams were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL requiring blood transfusion; serum creatinine and other biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a 2.9 × 2.5 × 2.4 cm polypoidal mass arising from the posterolateral wall of the bladder dome; both kidneys and the upper tracts appeared normal. Pre- and postvoid bladder volumes were 180 mL and 44 mL, respectively. Cystoscopy demonstrated an exophytic solid tumor measuring 1.5 × 2.0 cm on the anterior fundal wall, covered with slough. A deep transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological analysis revealed an adenocarcinoma composed of mucinous and signet-ring cell components. Thus, a secondary adenocarcinoma or a rare variant of primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder was suspected.

vignette:
A 50-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 1-week history of rapidly progressive gait disturbance. He reported no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss and had no history of smoking or known malignancy. On examination, he had full strength throughout all extremities but had decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward. He exhibited four beats of clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression. CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy, and laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. 

Given his rapidly progressive neurological decline, the decision was made to proceed urgently with surgical decompression, spinal stabilization, and tissue diagnosis.

vignette:
A 67‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless right vulvar mass extending into the right inguinal region. She first noted the lesion two years earlier, with gradual enlargement over the past four months. She denied pain, changes in appetite or bowel habits, urinary symptoms, weight loss, infection, or bleeding. She was post‐menopausal, had no history of hormone therapy, and did not smoke or drink alcohol.

On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. Inspection revealed a 12 cm, non‐tender mass of the right labia majora extending to the right groin, without erythema, lymphadenopathy, or signs of inflammation. Pelvic exam was otherwise normal.

Soft‐tissue ultrasound showed a well‐defined, hypoechoic solid mass measuring 90 × 44 × 55 mm in the right labia majora tracking into the inguinal canal, with mild peripheral blood flow on Doppler imaging. Routine laboratory results, including blood counts and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. The leading preoperative impression was a canal of Nuck hernia containing omental tissue.

vignette:
A 17-year-old single Turkish woman presented with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, and right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. She had no known exposure to tuberculosis. On examination she was afebrile with tender right lower abdominal quadrant and no rebound. Initial abdominal and chest radiographs were normal, and a bedside abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,200/μL, C-reactive protein of 12 mg/L, blood urea nitrogen of 35 mg/dL, and creatinine of 1.02 mg/dL. Urinalysis was unremarkable and a urine human chorionic gonadotropin test was negative. HIV testing was negative. While under observation, a second abdominopelvic ultrasound was interpreted as suggestive of retrocecal appendicitis. The patient was taken to the operating room via a McBurney’s incision. A 15 × 6 cm cystic mass with regular margins was found arising from the right tubo-ovarian complex; the appendix appeared clinically normal. The mass was excised intact, the tubo-ovarian structures were preserved, and on incision of the cyst wall purulent fluid was noted. Cultures were deferred until after the weekend.

A 61-year-old woman with type II diabetes presented with several days of urinary retention and inability to ambulate in the setting of a 1-year history of progressive lower-extremity weakness and a 100-lb unintentional weight loss. Her weakness began in the proximal left leg, gradually involved the right leg and both hands, and was accompanied by worsening numbness and tingling in her feet; she became wheelchair-dependent within 6 months. She denied pain, flank pain, hematuria, fevers, visual changes, speech or swallowing difficulty. On examination, she was alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II–XII were intact. She had bilateral weakness of hip flexors, knee flexors, knee extensors, and intrinsic hand muscles, with atrophy of the hands and thighs. Sensation to light touch was reduced in the feet, with slight impairment of vibration and proprioception. Reflexes were 2+ in the upper extremities and absent at the knees and ankles; plantar responses were flexor. Bladder catheterization yielded 1.8 L of retained urine. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count; sodium 117 mmol/L; chloride 87 mmol/L; blood urea nitrogen 0.89 mg/dL; creatinine 25 mg/dL. Urine was negative for protein or bacteria. A 67-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, active smoking (35 pack-years), a family history of ischaemic heart disease, and prior percutaneous coronary interventions (2008, 2017, 2022) for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction presented with Canadian Cardiovascular Society Class III angina. A 12-lead ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, Q waves in lead III, and biphasic T waves in leads III and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65% without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated patent stents in the circumflex artery, non-significant disease in the left anterior descending artery, and significant ostial right coronary artery stenosis with in-stent restenosis in the mid-segment, which was treated with three drug-eluting stents. After transfer to the intensive care unit, he complained of worsening chest pain; ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V3, and echocardiography remained normal. A second angiogram showed patent stents but subocclusion of the right coronary postero-lateral branch, successfully treated with balloon angioplasty, relieving his pain. Shortly thereafter, he developed recurrent sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation requiring seven external shocks and 15 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Post-resuscitation ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with persistent precordial ST-segment elevation and new QTc prolongation to 500 ms. Repeat echocardiography revealed akinesia of all apical segments, later extending to mid-segments, hyperkinesia of the basal segments, and severely reduced LVEF of 35%, leading to suspicion of takotsubo syndrome.

Intraoperatively, the mass was found in the right retroperitoneal space, tracking along the broad ligament and encasing the right external iliac artery; it was transected from the right uterine cornua. vignette:
A 25-year-old Hispanic woman of African descent, previously healthy and a non-smoker, presented with a 1-month history of dyspnea on exertion, intermittent dry cough, hyporexia, and unquantified intermittent fever. She delayed care until an acute worsening of dyspnea led to emergency department evaluation, where she developed acute respiratory failure and pulseless electrical activity arrest. After orotracheal intubation and stabilization, she was transferred to our institution.

On arrival, she was sedated on mechanical ventilation. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 200/140 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 bpm, temperature 36 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed anisocoria (right pupil 5 mm, left 3 mm), jugular venous distension, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral coarse rales; no skin lesions or peripheral edema were present.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right paratracheal mediastinal mass compressing and displacing the trachea to the left, with adjacent right upper-lobe infiltrates. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and neck demonstrated an 11 × 8.6 × 9.5 cm lobulated solid mass arising from the right thoracic operculum/pleura, with a nodular pleural component, mass effect on the right hilum, supra-aortic vessels, and superior vena cava, pneumomediastinum, left pneumothorax, and lytic destruction with cortical fracture of the T1 and T2 vertebrae. Centrilobular opacities in the left upper lobe suggested aspiration pneumonitis.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 13.47 × 10^3/µL (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 303 × 10^3/µL, INR 1.39, lactic acid 2.83 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 4.20 mg/dL, LDH 592 U/L, calcium 6.58 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.73 mg/dL; arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.30, PCO2 44.5 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3 22.3 mmol/L, BE –3.7 mmol/L, and SO2 98%. She received dexamethasone and piperacillin/tazobactam. Given the atypical imaging features and concern for possible hematologic malignancy, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy was planned to obtain adequate tissue.

vignette:
A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a right breast mass noted for more than 1 year, recently associated with skin ulceration. The mass had gradually enlarged, was hard in texture, non-tender, and mobile. One month before presentation, she observed a 3-cm area of skin breakdown with mild exudation and bleeding over the lesion.

On examination, a 4.5 × 5.5 cm irregular, poorly defined, hard mass was palpable at the 1 o’clock position in the right breast, 2.5 cm from the nipple, with overlying ulceration and slight serosanguinous discharge. The lesion was fairly mobile without palpable axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The left breast was normal.

Breast ultrasound and MRI both classified the lesion as BI-RADS category V. Chest CT demonstrated a right breast mass suggestive of malignancy. Serum breast tumor markers were within normal limits.

vignette:
A 67-year-old woman with a 4-day history of fever and cough was admitted to a local hospital, where SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR. Five days after admission, her respiratory status worsened, prompting intubation and transfer to the ICU. Her comorbidities included diabetes mellitus with dialysis-dependent nephropathy, angina, prior gastric cancer resection, and spinal‐canal stenosis; she was on an antiplatelet agent.  
On arrival: temperature 34 °C; blood pressure 110/65 mmHg; heart rate 102 beats/min; GCS E1VtM1 under deep sedation. Arterial blood gas (on pressure‐control ventilation: PEEP 8 cmH₂O, PiP 25 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 0.5) showed pH 7.309, PaCO₂ 41.5 mmHg, PaO₂ 78.2 mmHg.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 13,900/µL; CRP 13.1 mg/dL; D-dimer 7.25 µg/mL; APTT 170 s; INR 1.35.  
Chest CT: bilateral ground‐glass opacities with lower-lung predominance. Abdominal CT: no overt abnormalities or thromboembolism, but diffuse edema of the intestine, including the transverse colon, and marked sclerotic changes in abdominal vessels.  
She continued dexamethasone (6 mg/day) and commenced continuous renal replacement therapy. On ICU day 3, cefepime was started for ventilator-associated pneumonia. The APTT fell to 51.5 s, and prophylactic-dose unfractionated heparin was initiated to target an APTT of ~60 s.

vignette:
A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated. 

On day 8, she developed febrile neutropenia and received piperacillin–tazobactam. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species grew in blood cultures, prompting addition of teicoplanin. Persistent fever led to repeat cultures, which grew Enterococcus species, and teicoplanin was replaced with daptomycin. High-resolution chest CT showed nonspecific nodules under 1 cm, and serum galactomannan antigen was negative. After 10 days of fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 20/μL, she reported severe pain in her right arm radiating to her shoulder, suggesting herpes zoster; however, no vesicles were present. On examination, there was a very tender point in the upper lateral scapular region with an underlying vague mass. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a focal cystic necrotic lesion between the teres minor and teres major muscles.

vignette:
A 28-year-old Hispanic man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 10-day history of a pruritic eruption that began on the trunk and gradually spread to all extremities. He denied contact allergens, fever, or hyperhidrosis and had no prior history of atopic dermatitis, dermatophytosis, or hand eczema. On examination, he had scleral icterus and multiple dusky, thin plaques with a central collarette of scale on the face, neck, axillae, trunk, and extremities. On both hands and feet, there were hyperkeratotic plaques and deeply seated vesicles with a greenish-black hue, especially accentuated along the dermatoglyphic ridges. Laboratory testing showed total bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL (reference <1.2), direct bilirubin 17.7 mg/dL (<0.3), AST 78 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L. A punch biopsy of the right palm revealed psoriasiform epidermal acanthosis, intraepidermal spongiosis, hyperkeratosis with sparse perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, and a dilated eccrine duct containing amorphous pink material. Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.

vignette:
A female infant was born at 35 weeks 4 days’ gestation, weighing 2152 g. She was one of monochorionic diamniotic twins; her identical twin died in utero at 24 weeks. Fetal ultrasound had shown microcephaly and ventricular enlargement. Postnatal MRI of the head revealed microcephaly, marked enlargement of both lateral ventricles without signs of elevated intracranial pressure, and severe thinning of the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes; the temporal lobes, basal ganglia, thalamus, brain stem, and cerebellum were preserved. No intracranial hematoma or neoplastic lesions were seen. Family history was noncontributory. 

At 1 week of age, examination of the eyes showed very weak light reflexes bilaterally. The anterior chambers were slightly shallow, but there were no pupillary abnormalities, cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, or ptosis. Funduscopic examination revealed mild optic nerve pallor with suspected peripapillary double-ring sign. The fundus had a faint reddish tone; retinal vessels appeared normal in caliber and reached the periphery. No chorioretinal dysplasia was noted.

vignette:
A 46-year-old Japanese woman with a history of epilepsy presented with redness and swelling of the right breast. On examination, there was erythema and swelling in the lower right breast. Ultrasound revealed a 54 × 41 × 31 mm low-echo mass with partially unclear margins in the outer right breast. Biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type), high grade, ER+, PgR–, HER2 3+, Ki67 70%. Whole-body PET-CT revealed increased uptake in the right axilla, anterior mediastinum, left pleura, and liver, consistent with cT4dN3M1 stage IV breast cancer. She received four cycles of FEC chemotherapy, after which lesions nearly disappeared, and then trastuzumab plus pertuzumab with docetaxel, achieving a clinical complete response maintained for 23 months. Two years after treatment initiation, she developed a persistent headache. CT and MRI of the head revealed a 30-mm mass lesion in the right temporal lobe.
